clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant vitreoretinopathy caused by mutations in VCAN (versican), a component of the vitreous extracellular matrix, and unlike Stickler syndrome it lacks systemic skeletal and orofacial features
The defining sign is an optically empty vitreous cavity with avascular condensed membranes or veils, reflecting abnormal vitreous architecture
Chorioretinal atrophy, perivascular pigmentary change and progressive retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal thinning develop over time (the erosive vitreoretinopathy phenotype)
Patients may have myopia, early cataract, ectopic or dragged fovea and reduced night vision
Risk of retinal detachment is increased, though generally lower than in Stickler syndrome
Electroretinography may show progressive reduction in rod and cone responses as chorioretinal degeneration advances
Management is refractive correction, cataract surgery when indicated, lifelong monitoring for retinal detachment, and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Wagner syndrome is caused by dominant mutations in VCAN, which encodes versican, a large proteoglycan of the vitreous extracellular matrix. Abnormal splicing and altered versican disrupt the normal collagen-hyaluronan gel structure of the vitreous, producing liquefaction and the characteristic optically empty cavity with residual avascular membranes. Over time there is progressive chorioretinal and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, giving the erosive vitreoretinopathy picture, together with an increased predisposition to retinal detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Erosive vitreoretinopathy as a phenotypic variant
additionalInvestigations: Detailed slit-lamp and dilated examination documenting the optically empty vitreous and avascular veils
Optical coherence tomography for foveal ectopia and chorioretinal atrophy
Full-field electroretinography to monitor progressive photoreceptor dysfunction
Fundus autofluorescence for retinal pigment epithelium atrophy
Molecular genetic testing for VCAN mutations
redFlags: New floaters, flashes or field loss suggesting retinal detachment and needing urgent review
Progressive night blindness and field constriction from advancing chorioretinal atrophy
Early or rapidly progressive cataract affecting vision
Affected relatives requiring examination given dominant inheritance
reference.prognosis: Vision is often reasonable in early life but can decline with progressive chorioretinal atrophy, cataract and the risk of retinal detachment; long-term outcome varies and lifelong surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish Wagner syndrome from Stickler syndrome, which has systemic features and a higher detachment risk
Overlooking the increased retinal detachment risk during routine follow-up
Attributing the vitreous changes to simple myopic degeneration
Not offering genetic counselling for a dominantly inherited condition
management: Maintain lifelong vitreoretinal surveillance with regular dilated fundus examination given the raised risk of retinal detachment
Treat retinal breaks and tears prophylactically with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, and repair established detachment with vitreoretinal surgery
Correct the associated myopia with refraction and provide low-vision aids as chorioretinal atrophy advances
Undertake cataract surgery when visually significant, with careful planning because of the abnormal vitreous and detachment risk
Educate patients on the warning symptoms of retinal detachment and the need for urgent ophthalmic review
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant VCAN-related disease with family screening
Manage under a vitreoretinal specialist within a coordinated ophthalmic and genetics team
